title: AutoXPCR: Automated Multi-Objective Model Selection for Time Series Forecasting

problem.claim: Selecting forecasting models requires considering predictive error together with interpretability and resource consumption, because high-performing DNNs can be computationally intensive black boxes.

gap.claim: Few specialized AutoML methods have addressed the challenging domain of time series forecasting.

contributions.claim: AutoXPCR automatically produces DNN forecasting models while considering multiple objectives in an explainable fashion.
The approach uses meta-learning to estimate model performance across predictive error, complexity, and resource demand criteria.
AutoXPCR provides by-product explanations for recommendations and interactive control over the importance and trade-offs among the PCR criteria.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe AutoXPCR as a novel method for automated and explainable multi-objective DNN selection for forecasting.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report demonstrating AutoXPCR's practical feasibility across 108 forecasting data sets from various domains.
The authors report that AutoXPCR outperforms competing AutoML approaches, requires on average 20% of the computation costs, and recommends models with 85% of the empirical best quality.

narrative_sequence.summary: AutoML streamlines machine-learning model creation, but specialized approaches for time series forecasting are limited.
Although DNNs can achieve state-of-the-art forecasting performance, their computational intensity and opacity make predictive performance alone insufficient for model selection.
AutoXPCR is proposed as an automated and explainable method for producing DNN forecasters under multiple objectives, using meta-learning over predictive error, complexity, and resource demand.
The method supplies recommendation explanations and lets users interactively control criterion importance and trade-offs.
The authors report feasibility across 108 data sets and favorable average computation-cost and quality comparisons with competing AutoML approaches.

source_observation.claim: The authors report achieving 85% of empirical best quality with 20% of computation costs on average.

interpretation.claim: Automated selection may yield useful efficiency-quality trade-offs in the reported evaluation.

application.claim: When computation is constrained, compare candidate models using both achieved quality and selection cost.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the evaluation protocol, baseline details, or whether the reported averages generalize beyond the 108 data sets.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the forecasting tasks, data-set characteristics, or evaluation protocol.
The abstract does not define the meta-learning procedure or explainability mechanisms in technical detail.
The abstract does not identify the competing AutoML approaches or clarify how empirical best quality and computation costs were measured.
